# Hearing Smarter: A Scoping Review of Artificial Intelligence Implementation in Hearing Devices

## Abstract

Background/Objectives: Hearing loss affects over 1.57 billion people worldwide, and many who could benefit from hearing aids do not wear them. Poor speech understanding in noise is one of the main complaints, and several artificial intelligence (AI) models have been proposed to address it. This review aims to characterize AI applications in hearing devices and offers a framework for advancing from model development to clinical application. Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and APA PsycInfo were searched for peer-reviewed original studies published from 2010 to 2025. Data regarding AI task, architecture, input, training method, validation, and latency were collected for each model. Results: In total, 46 studies met the inclusion criteria. Speech enhancement was the most common task (58.7%), and deep neural networks were the most common architecture (34.8%). Training was predominantly offline (93.5%) and supervised (91.3%). Validation relied mainly on database/simulation (71.7%) and normal-hearing listeners (39.1%); only 1 model (2.2%) was validated using hearing-impaired listeners in real-world conditions. Ten models (21.7%) met the latency requirements for hearing aid use. Conclusions: AI has been applied across many hearing device tasks, but most models remain early in development. Clinical translation will require on-device implementation and real-world validation in hearing-impaired listeners.

## 1. Introduction

Hearing loss is among the most prevalent chronic health conditions worldwide. Over 1.57 billion people are estimated to be living with hearing loss, making it the third-leading cause of years lived with disability; this number is expected to increase to about 2.45 billion people by 2050 [1]. Hearing loss is associated with long-term health consequences, one of the most significant being dementia. A recent meta-analysis of 50 studies reported a 16% increase in dementia risk for every 10-decibel (dB) hearing loss [2]. In addition to cognitive decline, hearing loss is associated with social isolation, depression, reduced quality of life, and increased mortality [3]. Hearing aids are a primary treatment for hearing loss; however, their benefits depend heavily on consistent use. Some studies report that approximately 70 to 80% of adults who could benefit from hearing aids do not use them [3, 4, 5]. A major complaint with current hearing aids is that patients have difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments [3, 6].

This speech-in-noise problem is also the central limitation on signal processing with conventional hearing devices. Conventional single-microphone, non-spatial noise reduction algorithms have historically failed to improve speech intelligibility; these algorithms provide gains in listening comfort and listening effort, but they do not increase the number of understood words [3]. Multi-microphone spatial or beamforming processors have subsequently been implemented in hearing aids in an effort to overcome this limitation [7]. Most commercially available hearing aids today reduce noise using spatial selectivity, such as directional microphones and beamforming, which improves intelligibility only when the target and noise are spatially separated. Traditional amplification methods further propagate the speech-in-noise limitation by relying on fixed, rule-based fittings that are not individualized to the real-time acoustic environment [8, 9]. Artificial intelligence (AI) models, including traditional machine-learning (ML) and modern deep-learning approaches, have been proposed to address the persistent challenge of speech processing in complex acoustic environments.

AI methodologies proposed for hearing devices span a broad range of computational approaches. These approaches range from conventional machine learning (ML) and Bayesian frameworks to deep-learning architectures, which include deep neural networks (DNNs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), attentive recurrent networks (ARNs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and encoder–decoder architectures such as U-Net and Wave-U-Net. Researchers have also developed specialized hybrid architectures, including Deep Computational Auditory Scene Analysis (Deep CASA), Deep Complex Convolutional Recurrent Networks (DCCRNs), and Gated Convolutional Recurrent Networks (GCRNs), which combine multiple neural-network components to accomplish their tasks. The growing diversity of AI architectures reflects the increased efforts to overcome the limitations of traditional signal processing techniques and improve hearing device performance under real-world acoustic conditions.

Over the past decade, deep-learning methods have rapidly advanced acoustic signal processing for hearing devices. Deep-learning approaches, including DNNs, CNNs, RNNs, and related architectures, have significantly improved speech intelligibility and noise reduction for hearing devices [3, 10, 11]. Beyond denoising, AI has been applied to a rapidly expanding set of listening-related tasks, including speech enhancement, wind-noise suppression, acoustic-scene classification, alert-signal detection, speech segregation, source localization, feedback and occlusion management, audio–visual synthesis, adaptive dynamic range optimization, individualized auditory processing enhancement, and auditory attention decoding. The wide variety of applications suggests that AI could reshape how hearing devices process sound across nearly every stage of the acoustic pipeline.

Although AI applications are promising, a gap remains between algorithmic development and clinical translation. Current reviews of AI in audiology and otology focus on hearing screening, diagnosis, and device fitting, and several predate the recent surge in deep-learning methods [12, 13, 14]. Despite the rapid expansion of AI applications in hearing devices, the literature remains fragmented across different device types, acoustic-processing tasks, and model architectures. No comprehensive synthesis exists on how AI has been applied to hearing devices, which AI approaches have been investigated, and how AI models have been evaluated or implemented in current hearing devices. Accordingly, we conducted a scoping review to identify, characterize, and summarize AI applications in hearing devices; describe the AI architectures and learning approaches used; and examine how researchers have evaluated model performance across different acoustic tasks and validation settings. This review aims to provide a framework for model progression from development to clinical implementation.

## 2. Materials and Methods

We conducted a scoping review of the literature on AI applications in hearing devices following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines [15] (Supplementary Table S1). The study protocol was not registered. Our search strategy was developed in collaboration with a research librarian; the final search strategy is provided in Supplementary Table S2. The search was conducted on 26 August 2025, across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and APA PsycInfo databases. The literature search included all publications from January 2010 to August 2025. Search terms were chosen to capture all studies that developed or evaluated AI or ML models intended for use primarily in hearing devices.

Inclusion criteria included the development or evaluation of an AI model intended for use in or in conjunction with hearing aids. All AI model architectures were included in the analysis. Studies involving AI that did not clearly state or demonstrate application to these hearing devices were excluded. Only peer-reviewed, original research articles published in English were considered. The reference lists of included studies and relevant literature reviews were screened to identify additional eligible studies. Studies using AI models exclusively in cochlear implants were excluded.

Studies identified during the literature search were uploaded to Covidence (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia, available at www.covidence.org, last accessed on 10 September 2026), a web-based platform that helps facilitate citation screening, study selection, and data extraction between reviewers. The studies underwent de-duplication and title-and-abstract screening. Full-text articles were then reviewed against the inclusion and exclusion criteria before proceeding to data collection. At least two reviewers screened each study during title-and-abstract screening and full-text screening. A third reviewer resolved any differences between reviewers.

Studies that passed the full-text screening were included in the review, and data were extracted in Covidence using a standardized data-charting form developed by the authors. At least two reviewers independently reviewed each study during data collection. Reviewers resolved discrepancies through discussion and consensus.

The standardized data-charting form captured the following variables: author, year of publication, study design, primary AI task, AI model architecture, model input, reported or derived algorithmic latency, sample size, validation method, and acoustic environment (see Supplementary Table S3). The primary AI task was categorized by the principal hearing-related function that the algorithm performed. AI model architecture was classified based on the computational framework or algorithmic structure underlying the system. Model input referred to the primary data source processed by the model to perform its intended task. Algorithmic latency was defined as the time required for the AI model to process input data and generate an output during signal processing, excluding any hardware-related delays that contribute to total end-to-end latency. The validation method was categorized according to the approach used to evaluate model performance on data not used during training. The acoustic environment was categorized based on the listening conditions evaluated in each study.

Objective outcomes, subjective outcomes, and future directions were described narratively. Objective outcomes included quantifiable measures of model performance, whereas subjective outcomes included participant-reported assessment of the model’s perceived effectiveness.

Algorithmic latency was used to assess whether the AI model was potentially feasible within hearing aid latency requirements. Each model was classified against the latency budget of 5 to 10 milliseconds (ms), representing the upper limit of processing delay before self-voice coloration, echo, and sound quality degradation become perceptible [16]. Feasibility was categorized as “Yes,” “Partial/Conditional,” “No,” “Unable to Determine,” or “Not Applicable.” A model was categorized as “Partial/Conditional” when the model could meet the latency requirement only under specific stated conditions.

The data were summarized, and all figures and tables were created using Microsoft Excel for Microsoft 365 (version 2806; Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA).

## 3. Results

In total, 572 studies were identified through database and citation searches. After removing duplicates, 405 studies underwent title-and-abstract screening, and 79 full-text studies
